Abstract—Growing rates of crop disease and insect infestations
are threatening the overall health of the agricultural industry
as well as food production worldwide, and traditional methods
for monitoring crops through visual inspection are often too
time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale up. This paper
presents an AI-based system capable of diagnosing crop leaf
health in real-time using state-of-the-art computer vision and
deep learning technologies. The framework implemented uses
a multi-step pipeline composed of an object detection model, a
classification model and a vision-based reasoning system; where
the object detection portion of the workflow uses a YOLOv8
model to determine the location of infected areas, an automated
region-of-interest extraction tool is then used to extract from
the image the regions of interest so as to improve the overall
accuracy of disease detection.

A second EfficientNet based model
is then used to estimate the severity of the disease found in
the infected area, while an additional vision-based reasoning
module is added that looks for visual patterns associated with pest
infestations in order to provide contextual information to assist
with the diagnosis process. The methodology used to develop this
framework includes (1) preprocessing image datasets, (2) training
the models on agricultural datasets and (3) deploying an end-
to-end inference pipeline that can process user provided inputs
through the detection, feature extraction, and diagnosis phases. Preliminary experimental results show high levels of accuracy in
the detection of disease and classification of severity, in addition
to the implementation of multiple models in a single frame-
work resulting in greater problem-solving capabilities overall.The
proposed system provides a scalable and efficient solution for
intelligent crop monitoring, enabling early disease detection and
supporting data-driven decision making in agricultural practices. Index Terms—Artificial Intelligence, Plant Disease Detection,
YOLOv8, EfficientNet, Computer Vision, Deep Learning, Preci-
sion Agriculture
I. INTRODUCTION
Agriculture is the foundation in providing food security
and economic sustainability across the globe, but diseases
like plant disease, pests are key factors of crop loss (yield
& quality). Good crop management is built on early disease
detection and a correct diagnosis of the pathogen involved. Ironically, actual inspection by experts is time-consuming,
biased and extremely difficult to scale in large-scale farmland
[1], [5]. These restrictions render real time diagnosis an urgent
necessity for intelligent and automated systems.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has made great
strides in the fields of computer vision and deep learning,
which has resulted in promising progress in image-based plant
disease detection. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have
shown great ability in extracting complex visual features and
high classification accuracy in many agricultural datasets [10],
[13] . The availability of large annotated datasets and the use
of transfer learning techniques have further accelerated the
development of automated plant health monitoring systems
[11], [12] . However, despite these advances, most of the
existing methods are limited to the task of image classification
and do not provide spatial localization of infected regions,
which reduces interpretability and practical usability in real
world scenarios [6], [18]. Real-time localization of regions in images affected by
disease has been facilitated by object detection frameworks
such as YOLO, improving accuracy and interpretability [7],
[8]. However, some existing systems lack combination of
detection with advanced diagnosis features such as severity
estimation and contextual analysis [2]. In addition, traditional
image processing techniques are not robust to complicated
environmental conditions, e.g. lighting changes, background

noise and occlusions [20] . These challenges call for the
development of more comprehensive and robust diagnostic
frameworks. In this context, the integration of several deep learning
models into a single pipeline has become a promising tech-
nique to improve the diagnostic performance. More sophisti-
cated architectures like EfficientNet offer better accuracy and
computational efficiency for real-time applications [9]. Hybrid
models combining convolutional models with advanced learn-
ing techniques have shown improved performance for complex
recognition tasks [3], [4]. The combination of spatial detection,
feature extraction, and contextual reasoning can be utilized to
construct a more robust and scalable system for plant disease
diagnostics. An AI system was developed to improve the accuracy and
speed of recognising how healthy a plant’s leaf is. This system
has four main features: an object detector for determining
where to find the leaf, a classifier using deep learning to assess
how bad the leaf is, and two other methods to help improve
diagnostic reliability. Each feature can be used separately or
combined for a modular configuration for scalability and field
deployment. These features are the result of some new, novel
approaches to developing a multi-model diagnostic system,
achieving greater accuracy as a result of using multiple algo-
rithms together, and a scalable solution to enable intelligent
agricultural decision making. II. LITERATURE REVIEW
Many researchers have looked into detecting plant diseases
through various ways ranging from traditional approaches
involving image processing to applying deep learning methods.

The earlier methods focused mainly on handcrafted feature
extraction methods where color, texture and shape were the
commonly used features, thus allowing researchers to find
patterns of disease development based on visible character-
istics in plant leaves. Traditional methods provide the ability
to process images quickly; however, traditional methodologies
do not perform well, due to illumination changes, background
interference and large-scale variability characteristics, result-
ing in poor performance in terms of generalisation [20]. With the advent of deep learning, in particular convolutional
neural networks (CNN), the field of plant disease classification
tasks has witnessed remarkable progress. Foundational works
demonstrated that deep CNN architectures are effective in
image recognition, enabling automated feature extraction and
higher classification accuracy [10], [16]. The same models
were used in later studies on agricultural datasets where
promising results were reported in terms of disease identifica-
tion in various types of crops [11], [13] . Transfer learning was
used to boost model performance using pre-trained networks,
reducing the dependence on massive labeled datasets [6], [17]. Recent studies are aimed at developing architectures that
can increase efficiency and accuracy in existing models. The
introduction of compound scaling by EfficientNet have estab-
lished a new paradigm of optimizing depth as well as width &
resolution; leading to superior performance with reduced num-
ber of overall parameters for each model [9]. Research using
EfficientNet for classification of plant diseases have yielded
greater levels of generalization and accuracy than traditional
CNN models [3] .

Convolutional Neural Network models
paired with vision transformers have also shown greater ability
to capture local & global features leading to improvements in
recognition performance as well [4]. Overall, comprehensive
reviews show increased adoption of deep learning methods in
agriculture while identifying many opportunities including but
not limited to implementation scalability and interpretability
[1], [5] issues. There are a lot of object detection frameworks now that try
to fix the problems with models that only do classification. Methods like R-CNN that look at parts of an image have
given us the location of objects in images but they took a long
time to work [14]. The YOLO framework has changed object
detection by giving us image processing and correct detection
which makes it useful for real life [7]. The new versions of
YOLO like YOLOv5 and YOLOv8 have made object detection
faster and more precise, which is really helpful for farmers
who want to detect crop diseases in their fields using YOLO. YOLO has really helped farmers use YOLO for crop disease
detection, in their fields [2], [8]. Current models have made great progress; however most
current models are limited to one function (either detection or
classification), and most lack integration of various diagnostic
capabilities. Many current models do not include either sever-
ity estimation or contextual analysis needed to make effective,
well-informed decisions in agricultural settings. Various issues
persist in the form of changing conditions, occlusions, and
limitations in data sets that continue to affect model perfor-
mance.

As such, a multi-stage, comprehensive framework that
includes detection, classification, and higher-order reasoning
is necessary for developing reliable, valid, and interpretable
plant health diagnosis. TABLE I

III. PROPOSED SYSTEM OVERVIEW
This new system is a multi-stage deep learning system to
assist in the diagnosis of plant leaf disease and offers an
alternative to the traditional single model approach. Many
current models rely on using convolutional neural networks
(CNN) to conduct image-level classification; while CNNs are
good at classifying images they do not take into consideration

any form of spatial context and struggle when trying to
identify localized patterns of disease [6], [18]. There are
many examples of deep learning based models reaching a
high level of classification accuracy [1], [5], however, as they
do not facilitate region-based analysis they may offer limited
objectivity and reliability for diagnosis when looking at single
images. The system has been designed to combine detection and
identification into one process in order to address the chal-
lenges associated with this type of analysis. Using object
detection models like YOLO, it is possible to provide real-
time identification of areas of interest (i.e., affected) within
a given image [7], [8]. In conjunction, using EfficientNet-
based architectures for classification [3], [9] can provide a
highly accurate representation of the identified areas and
therefore combine both spatial and semantic knowledge about
the disease-affected plants being analyzed. Sequential options for processing an input image include
preprocessing, detection, region extraction, and classification. Each stage transforms the data representation for the next
stage and strengthens the final result’s robustness and features. The multi-stage model corresponds to newly developed hybrid
deep learning systems with better performance through inte-
gration of models [4]. The modular framework for the system
provides scalability and deployment to real-world settings (as
detailed in Table II). A. System Description
The proposed system is an end-to-end pipeline transforming
the original input images into structured diagnostic output. At the beginning of the pipeline, the input images will be
preprocessed so that they can be normalized and resized to
create an image set with consistent dimensions.

Once the
images are preprocessed and normalized, they will be passed
to the real-time object detection model, which will localize
infected areas by locating them within the overall image of
the leaf. This type of region-aware analysis is the primary
shortcoming of most current CNN models, which process
whole images without regard to their spatial distributions. [11],
[13]. Once the localised areas have been identified; the areas
are separated using an automatic crop process that removes
noise (from the background). This reduces background noise
and improves the relevance of identifying features used in the
classification process. The analysis of the areas; is done using
an EfficientNet-based deep learning model, which produces
predictions for the season type and severity of the diseases. The EfficientNet model uses a compound scaling algorithm
that improves accuracy while improving calculation efficiency.
[9]. Ultimately the outputs coming from the detection and
classification will be combined to form an overall diagnostic
output. The overall accuracy of the system is improved by
integrating the outputs from several processing stages instead
of doing them in a single step approach. The use of both
transfer learning and/or pre-trained models can also further
enhance its accuracy in conditions where agricultural datasets
are scarce. [6], [17]. B. Key Features
The system suggested here has a multi-stage processing
pipeline to implement object detection and classification to
manage the entire process of diagnosing plant diseases. With
this multi-stage, region-aware analysis, it is possible to locate
infected areas accurately and significantly increase the inter-
pretability and accuracy of the diagnosis, unlike conventional
image-based classification methods.

The main element of the design is an automatic mechanism
to extract regions of interest so as to classify only the areas
where disease exists. Thus, greatly reducing the impact of
background noise and irrelevant characteristics, which has
been a common limitation of most ”classic” deep learning
systems trained on full images. [11], [13]. This system significantly benefits from the power of con-
temporary deep learning systems by using two distinct yet
complementary parts - YOLO-based real-time object detection
[2], [8] and EfficientNet-based classification models [3], [9]. The combination of both provides the capability to achieve
both high levels of precision and outstanding computational
efficiency in order to enable real-time agricultural applications. The Independence of each component allows for greater
ease in both scaling and updating each component, allowing
new technologies and processing methods as they become
available (ex. transformers, multimodal processing, and hybrid
DL systems) to be adopted into the system because they
represent improvements in their respective areas through the
course of time. [4]. C. Novelty
A new unified multi-stage diagnostic framework is proposed
that integrates regional detection and classification in order to
solve some of the major limitations of current plant disease
detection technologies. Unlike traditional methods which clas-
sify an entire image and then make a prediction based on this
global classification [10], [13], the new method incorporates
analysis of specific regions of interest so that predictions are
made based on localised characteristics of a disease.

Utilizing an automatic method for isolating (extracting)
infected areas from the entire scanned image through region-
of-interest extraction significantly improves feature quality (by
isolating the infected areas) which provides for better overall
classification accuracy and fewer false predictions, especially
in more complicated areas with much variability in the back-
ground when compared to what would normally occur with
non-complex (non-variability) and/or clean (uncontaminated
with background clutter). The framework offers both spatial and semantic capabilities
by utilizing a dual-modal based approach with object detection
for classification of data. Most of the available YOLO type
detection only cover detection [2] capabilities. The proposed
expansion will further help to determine disease severity and improve diagnostic evaluations through the addition of an
estimation process to the detection process. The proposed design ultimately focuses on modularity and
the potential for increased scalability, offering the flexibility
of adding various types of models to be deployed in real-time. Combining region-aware processing, multi-model integration,
and extensible architecture makes our system unique compared
to current solutions. This combination provides a more reliable
and thorough method for the intelligent diagnosis of diseases
in plants.

IV. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
The architecture of this system is built as a systematic
multistage pipeline with the ability to combine preprocessing,
spatial feature detect, and diagnostic analysis into one com-
plete real time system for the identification of disease in plants. This proposed architecture provides for the combination of
the two processes within one workflow, as opposed to most
traditional architectures which view detection and classifica-
tion as independent functions, leading to better diagnostic
accuracy and interpretability. By using an object detection
system model for localization and a DCNN for classification,
the architecture achieves the needed degree of both spatial and
semantic understanding of plant disease occurrences. [2], [3],
[8]. The architectural design uses a modular approach whereby
every module performs a distinct operation and communicates
effortlessly with all other modules. Modularity provides the
capability to scale up or down to accommodate a variety of
different data sets as well as deployment settings.

Integration
of processing focused on multiple regions of interest (ROI)
and multi-model integration offers an alternative to classic
convolutional neural networks (CNN), which treat an entire
image as one unit without considering spatial context. [6],
[18]. The complete structure of the system is illustrated in
Fig. 1. A. Architecture Overview
There are three main levels of architecture: the in-
put/preprocessing level, the detection level and the diagnostic
level. The input level has responsibility for obtaining the
leaf picture as well as conducting initial preprocessing of
that image (e.g., resizing and normalising). This is done to
ensure that all of the images being processed have similar
appearance when used in model training, in order to provide
better consistency in the data when being used, therefore
improving the performance of the model. By using a YOLO-based model for real-time object de-
tection, the detection layer provides spatial awareness to the
system and allows it to zone in on the pertinent parts of an
image [7], [8] instead of processing the full image as one large
block of data. The result is that infected areas are identified
and isolated to improve the overall quality of the features that
are extracted and reduce the amount of background noise from
the image. The extracted areas go through a classification and analysis
process in the diagnostic section. A deep convulutional model
based on EfficientNet, with optimised scaling and high predic-
tion accuracy [3], [9], was used to determine how severe the
disease is, as well as what type of disease the patient has. An
overall diagnostic result is created by merging outputs from
different levels.

The separate levels work together while being
independent of one another and also integrate with one another
so that data can flow through all levels efficiently and in real-
time. Multi-Stage Feature Fusion

B. Workflow Explanation
A user interface (UI) enables you to take a photo of a leaf. We send the photo to our processing backend server. The photo
undergoes preprocessing, which ensures it has the same size
and quality. By allowing the model to be tested with different
input conditions, we guarantee that these will not introduce
variance in the model’s ability to predict the expected outcome. Following a picture being taken by the camera, it will be
sent to a machine that can identify diseased portions of the
picture with a YOLO model to help locate the infection. This
is an important part of making a correct diagnosis. After
determining where the infected area is, the machine can then
remove the infected portions of the picture. The camera is
used to capture an image and the YOLO-based model is used
to assist the machine in identifying the infected portion of the
image. The classification module then analyses the extracted re-
gions, predicting the disease category and the degree of
severity. For this stage, it uses deep convolutional networks
(DCN) to extract high-level features from the region images
and provide accurate predictions based on these features. The
predicted outputs from both detection/identification (DAI) and
classification (CL) form the basis for making a final diagnosis
in the diagnostic module, which integrates the two previous
steps’ results into one single outcome.

The processed output
is then received by the user’s interface as useful means of
actionable and informative insight regarding the health of the
plants. The structured data processing workflow maximizes ef-
ficiency by reducing the occurrence of false predictive outputs, and therefore increasing the overall reliability of the real-time
agricultural systems. Fig. 1. Overall System Architecture
V. METHODOLOGY
Methodology consists of a structured multi-step pipeline
for plant leaf disease detection and assessment. It consists of
data preparation, spatial detection, region-oriented processing,
and classification. The proposed system is created to main-
tain robustness across many different input datasets. This is
done by using a standardised set of preprocessing techniques
in conjunction with advanced deep learning models. The
methodology focuses on refining the input data sequentially
to enhance feature quality and predictive accuracy. A. Data Collection
To ensure diversity and generalization when training mod-
els, a range of publically available agriculture datasets is used
by the system. The principal data sets used are the PlantVillage
data set, which contains labeled photos of diseased and healthy
plant leaves that were taken under controlled environments;
and the PlantWild data set that has real world photos of plants
taken under different natural environments including different
types of lighting, occlusion and diverse backgrounds. The
ability of the model to learn both patterns in structure and
patterns in randomness will give it the robustness necessary
for practical use. The importance of using diverse datasets to
prevent overfitting and enhance model generalization has been
well documented in recent literature. [1], [5]. B.

Data Preprocessing
Having quality input data helps increase model performance
through model improvement processes. Collecting quality data
is important in that it helps create datasets of uniform images
and eliminates unnecessary data. Before using images for
training, the images must be preprocessed to increase prob-
ability of being compared with other images when measuring
outcome. Next, the images must be cleaned so the training
does not fail due to low-quality images. Model performance
will be improved if the number of images available for training
increase than the total number of images available for use in
training. Normalization is used to adjust pixel values so they are all
on an equal range and help to provide consistent convergence
while training a model. In deep learning this is especially
beneficial because it helps alleviate the effects of different
lighting conditions on the variations in pixel values. Also,
formatting procedures are performed to properly organize the
data base into the training and validation before the model can
be run for the purposes of evaluation. Rotation, flipping, and scaling, some augmentation tech-
niques that simulate the real world to help apply more variance
to the model and help generalize better on data that was never
presented to the model in its training set, further improve the
robustness of the model. C. Model Design
The multi-stage design model’s architecture consists of
detection and classification components that are separated
into multiple tiers. The first tier is made up of the object-
detection module using the YOLO architecture. This module
finds and locates disease-affected areas inside an input image,
and YOLO was chosen because of its high accuracy rate and
ability to provide real-time results. [7], [8].

In the second phase of the extraction process, a region
extraction system extracts all of the isolated regions so there is
only an area of interest within the image to perform any further
analysis. This greatly improves the quality of any features
because it eliminates any background noise. The last module is a classification module that uses Ef-
ficientNet architecture to predict disease type and severity. EfficientNet is the chosen model for its optimized scaling
strategy, and EfficientNet has superior performance levels
compared to all other choices in image classification tasks [3], [9]. The ability to integrate both detection and classifi-
cation models allows the system to capture both spatial and
semantic information thus increasing the overall accuracy of
the diagnosis. The outputs of each stage are aggregated using a diagnostic
aggregation procedure to produce a single output that contains
both localization and classification information. D. Feature Extraction
Deep learning models provide implicit feature extraction,
as they automatically generate hierarchical representations of
input data. During the detection phase, convolutional layers
extract spatial features (e.g., boundaries of regions, object
localization) used to determine the location of any infected
areas on an image of a leaf.

VI. IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
The proposal involves a modular real-time inference system
that combines a deep learning algorithm with an API for
efficient plant disease diagnosis. Low latency processing,
scalability, and smooth interactions between components are
the key design considerations for this system. Each step
in the process (feeder operation, pre-processing, detection,
classification and final result generation) will be developed as
individual components using a service-oriented architecture.

Endpoints That Transmit Input Images from the User Interface
to the API endpoints for Processing & Validation and Prepro-

Multiple Deployment Environments such as Web-Based Sys-
tems and Edge Systems. Infected Areas are located through a process called De-
tection. To do this, a Real Time infection detection method
uses a YOLO-based Detection Method for the localization
of the location of Infected Areas. The YOLO Architecture
has been established as a leading objective detection method
[7], [8], and new architectures like YOLOv8 also provide
higher accuracy for agricultural detection applications [2]. The
Detection Method outputs bounding boxes around infected
areas with a probability score which is later filtered for low
confidence probabilities using a filter based on predetermined
thresholds. Once the detected areas of interest have been identified, a
mechanism will allow for the extraction of regions associated
with each of those areas, so that only these regions—i.e., those
that relate to diseases—are used in future processing. This step
removes any background interference and enhances the quality
of features in comparison to traditional classification models
that operate over the entire image space. [11], [13]. The classification phase uses a convolution neural network
based on EfficientNet which is known for its scaled efficiency
and for being a high performing model for image classification
applications [3], [9] .

Using transfer learning, the EfficientNet
Model is trained with pre-trained features and adjusted appro-
priately for agricultural data sets in order to generate class
probabilities to assist with confidence decision making [6],
[17]. The second (or intermediate) evaluation layer receives out-
put from each of the previous detection and classification lay-
ers. Confirmation of prediction reliability takes place through
the review of confidence levels and consistency checks; there-
fore, predicted severity of disease is representative of the size
of the areas detected as infected, i.e., logical consistency of
final output. Compared to the approach that uses only one
model, this process provides greater assurance of prediction
reliability using multiple stages of validation. [1], [5]. In addition to a reasoning module that allows the interpreta-
tion of model outputs and generation of structured diagnostic
insights, there is an added benefit of mapping the predicted
output of the model to domain-related knowns to improve the
interpretability of the model and support real world decision
making for agricultural applications. The system has been designed to load models and utilize
them effectively. The system loads models once and then
repeatedly uses them to save time as well. A computer can
utilize a specific component known as a graphics processing
unit (GPU) to work at a faster rate. If your computer is weak or
not very powerful, it can run on CPU as well. The system has
also been designed using flexibility so future ideas or models
will be able to run; examples include joint use of convolutional
and transformer model types. [4].

A. System Workflow
The system workflow consists of an ordered container
for processing raw image inputs and transforming them into
trustable diagnosis outputs via a series of processing phases
(sequential processes). Each phase has an intended purpose
of improving the input data through repeated processing so
that the resulting features are of high quality, making accurate
predictions possible and resulting in efficient inference. Input Acquisition: The process of getting an image of a
leaf starts with uploading it via a user interface. After being
uploaded, the image is sent to the backend server via an API
call, where subsequent checks will be made on the base file
type, resolution and integrity of the file.

Preprocessing: The acquired image undergoes preprocess-
ing operations, including resizing to a fixed resolution, nor-
malization of pixel values, and conversion into tensor format. These steps standardize the input data and reduce variability
caused by environmental factors such as illumination changes
and background noise. Detection: We send the prepared image through the part
of the system that will search for diseases. The tool used
by this part of the system to identify and indicate where the
infection is found on the image is called YOLO. When YOLO
determines an infection’s location, it draws a box around the
area on the image, gives a probability score of the likelihood
of infection at that area, and identifies which areas do not
have a probability score (indicating we can trust YOLO’s
determination of that area as an infection site). YOLO is
excellent at identifying infection locations within the image. Region Extraction: The system uses the coordinates of
the bounding boxes to select the areas on the images that
are related to infection. This means that we can remove the
background, where there are no disease-related areas of the
image, and focus on those regions that have clarity of features,
with less interference from any background that is not related
to the disease itself. Classification: An EfficientNet-based classification algo-
rithm will process the regions extracted from the images and
will provide predictions on the disease classification as well
as determines how severe it may be. This classification data
is further utilized to create probability distributions for each
of their respective disease classes and will allow for clinical
decision-making through utilizing probability distributions and
therefore improving diagnostic accuracy.

Evaluation and Aggregation: At this point, detection
and classification output are consolidated for a final output
prediction that is consistent and reliable. Confidence thresholds
can be used, while spatial characteristics (in this case infected
area size) can be correlated with severity predictions to estab-
lish logical consistency among predictions. Validation in this
manner contributes to increase robustness and the elimination
of false positives. Output Generation: The results from this stage are pack-
aged into a structured output that includes all the calculated
metrics and summarizes the total number of areas identified
for investigation, a corresponding predicted diagnosis with
associated severity level and associated level of certainty. The
results will be sent to the user interface as well as elaborate on
the nature of the findings in order to give clear and actionable
information related to the diagnosis. VII. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
By utilizing both an experimental and real-world environ-
ment to evaluate the performance of the newly developed
multi-phase diagnostic for detecting plant diseases, the centre
looks at detection accuracy, classification performance and
overall reliability of prediction. Both the testing experiment
will use various agricultural datasets from standard databases
and use the commonly used measures in computer vision and
deep learning methods. A. Dataset Description
The evaluation of the proposed system is conducted using
two complementary datasets to ensure both robustness and
generalization capability. PlantVillage Dataset: The PlantVillage dataset is utilized
as a key benchmark dataset.

It contains a large volume of
accurate and labelled pictures of plants taken in a consistent
environment and have a uniform background (i.e., they are all in the same lighting conditions, and are photographed at the
same angle). Having this kind of dataset means the model can
learn clear and well-defined disease patterns. The dataset is
therefore appropriate for initial training and validation. [11],
[12]. PlantWild Dataset: The PlantWild dataset has been used
for evaluation purposes in order to test real-world application
performance of the computer vision system. The dataset con-
sists of images taken in an uncontrolled natural environment. This includes variability in lighting, background complexity,
occlusion, and leaf orientation. The addition of this variability
produces real-world challenges that allow the computer vision
system to be evaluated for generalization and robustness in
practical use. [1], [5]. Data Splitting and Augmentation: There are three sub-

B. Comparative Analysis
The comparative assessment performed compares the vari-
ous methods available for identifying diseases affecting plants. Image processing systems based on traditional methods show
poor identification performance due to their inability of being
able to account for changes within the surrounding envi-
ronment. Methods that are based on Convolutional Neural
Networks provide greater accuracy than traditional methods;
however, provide little spatial awareness. Detection-based sys-
tems allow for some form of localization, but are not able
to fully capture the features associated with different plant
diseases when utilized on their own. Combining detection with classification creates a single
system; both spatial analysis and semantics can be performed
using this system. Because of this combination, the prediction
results will now be better than before, especially under condi-
tions of complexity, such as varying amounts of background
noise and variability that are present in real-world scenarios.

Experimental findings indicate that the proposed multi-
stage framework enhances diagnostic performance through a
combination of spatial detection and classification. By first
localizing the area of the affected area before performing a
classification, it will enable feature extraction to focus on the
relevant sections of the image, thus avoiding any background
noise and therefore improving the prediction results. The
region-aware (localised) approach provides a direct resolution
to one of the key limitations that are experienced with standard
(classical) CNN models, which work with whole images
without accounting for spatial relationships [6], [18].

The
overall increase in accuracy provides strong evidence of the
effectiveness of integrating detection with classification in a
single pipeline. Detection and classification blocks are complementary to
one another. The detection block accurately locates infected
areas, while the classification block extracts high-level seman-
tic features to improve the accuracy of disease diagnosis [7],
[8]. These two blocks work together to create both spatial
and semantic awareness of plant diseases [3], [9]. The third
evaluation block also works to enhance the reliability of
predictions by filtering out low reliability predictions and
aligning predicted severity of infection with the actual infected
area; this follows recent trends in deep learning integration [1],
[5]. X. FUTURE SCOPE
Future studies might focus on implementing advanced deep
learning structures (transformer-style visual models or hybrid
architectures made up of convolutional neural networks and
transformers) to the system. Models with these types of
architectures seem to perform better than existing architec-
tures in establishing complex feature relationships [4]. Future
research will also incorporate multi-modal inputs, such as
environmental conditions (e.g., temp, humidity, and soil),
which will help improve diagnostic accuracy by providing ad-
ditional disease/pest contextual information, apart from visual
characteristics of disease/pest features. The system may be adapted to allow for large-scale agricul-
tural use by expanding its cloud infrastructure and distributed
processing capabilities from a deployment standpoint.

By
using optimized models in an edge deployment, it is now
possible to offer real-time diagnostic capabilities in resource-
constrained settings, consistent with recent trends toward using
edge AI for agricultural systems [2]. In addition, developing
a dataset to include broader ranges of crop types and disease
categories will enhance the generalization of models, and using
explainable AI methods will improve users’ understanding of
and confidence in the predictions made. XI. CONCLUSION
Using a unified pipeline to combine detection of object to
classification with in one pipeline. The proposed approach
has resolved some of the key limitations found in the current
methods. By using regional analysis, the proposed methodol-
ogy allows the system to concentrate on regions with diseased
tissue rather than having to process the entire image. The use
of both YOLO for localisation of an object and EfficientNet
for accurate classification, provides improved overall diagnosis
performance base on both location and types of disease. Results from the experiment demonstrated that the proposed
system meets all criteria for accuracy and reliability per all
measures of evaluation used to assess it. In combination with
detection and classification, they contribute to the improve-
ment of prediction stability by diminishing the impact of noisy
background on predictions and enhancing the significance of
features. Additionally, our results provide evidence of the
generalization properties of the system, since it was able to
accurately analyze both artificial and natural samples. These
factors indicate that the system is a viable tool for agricultural
use in a practical setting.

Farmers can identify agricultural disease outbreaks prior
to them causing significant agricultural damage by using our
agricultural monitoring systems. You’ll gain quicker, depend-
